writingModel: What Went Wrong with the WKU Library Renovation? An Analytical Assessment

In late 2024, the WKU central library underwent a six-month renovation. The project ran three months over schedule and significantly over budget. The original deadline must have seemed achievable at the planning stage — the project scope was not unusual for a building of this size. Yet the delays were extensive. This essay analyses what went wrong, what should have been done differently, and what can be learned for future projects.

Several factors must have contributed to the overrun. The initial contractor, who was responsible for the structural work, was replaced after two months. This replacement can't have been planned — it suggests a serious performance failure that should have been identified earlier in the tendering process. The original tender may have been too focused on cost, and the lowest bidder might not have had the capacity to deliver on time.

Furthermore, the procurement of materials appears to have been poorly coordinated. Delays in material delivery must have cascaded, pushing subsequent phases back. The project manager's records, which have since been reviewed, suggest that problems were being identified internally but weren't being escalated. Someone should have raised these concerns with senior management much earlier.
What Could Have Been Done Differently

Several missed opportunities can be identified. First, the university could have engaged a project management consultant from the outset. Given the scale and importance of the renovation, this oversight is surprising. Second, the tendering process ought to have included stricter capacity requirements — the lowest bid should have been rejected on those grounds alone.
Third, a contingency budget should have been established at the start. None was apparently set aside. The project needn't have failed so expensively had basic risk mitigation been applied.

The evidence suggests that the overrun was largely avoidable. The project must have failed for a combination of reasons: a weak initial contractor, poor procurement coordination, and inadequate escalation of early warning signs. More attention should have been paid to risk management from the beginning. Future renovations of comparable scale should be subject to independent oversight throughout.
